title: Traffic congestion: possible solutions to an increasing problem

paragraphs.text: Traffic congestion has long been a feature of large and growing metropolitan areas across the world. Peak-hour traffic congestion is an inherent aspect of modern society yet, in spite of repeated bids to remedy the situation, the problem seems to be worsening. Congestion poses a significant urban planning challenge, and the public have often been frustrated by policymakers’ failures when trying to resolve the problem. Although governments may never be able to eliminate it entirely, there are several ways cities and states might move to curb congestion.

Traffic congestion stems from modern society's basic mobility problem: the widespread desires of people to pursue certain goals at certain times each day. The smooth operation of both the economy and school systems requires that people work, attend school, and run errands during approximately the same time period so they can interact with each other. The result of this is that too many people want to move at the same time, which inevitably overloads roads and other transit systems. That basic requirement cannot be altered without crippling our economy and society. The same problem exists in every major metropolitan area worldwide.

In the USA, the vast majority of people seeking to move during rush hours use private automotive vehicles, for two reasons. One is that most US citizens reside in sprawling, thinly populated residential areas that publicly funded transit networks cannot efficiently serve. The second is that private vehicles are more comfortable, faster, more convenient, and more appropriate for the individual performing multiple tasks on a single trip than almost any form of public transit. As household incomes rise worldwide, people increasingly shift from slower, less expensive modes of movement to privately owned vehicles. Road systems designed for far fewer vehicles then lack the necessary capacity to absorb peak-hour traffic loads, and people are forced to wait in line for limited road space — the definition of congestion. There are four ways of coping with this mobility challenge, but all of them have issues of their own.

Governments can charge people to enter some or all lanes on major commuting roads during peak hours. If tolls were set at the optimum level and collected electronically with ‘smart cards,’ vehicle numbers on each major road during peak hours could, in theory, be reduced. Vehicles could then move at higher speeds allowing more people to travel per lane per hour than current, heavily congested conditions do. Although transportation economists have long been proponents of this tactic, it is difficult politically because tolls would favor wealthier or subsidized drivers and would harm poor ones. Most US citizens would therefore oppose them, partly because they believe they would be at a disadvantage.

Whenever road tolls have been tried elsewhere, people have tended to perceive them as an extra tax, forcing them to pay for something they believe they have already paid for through gasoline taxes. For these reasons, few politicians advocate this tactic. The only precedents worldwide have been road-pricing schemes adopted in Singapore, Norway, and London. These schemes target congestion in crowded downtowns, which is not the kind of congestion experienced on major arterial roads in the US.

The second approach would be to expand public transit capacity to the extent that there would no longer be too much demand for roads during peak hours. But in the United States in 2000, for example, only 4.7 percent of all commuters utilised public transit. A major reason is that most such commuting is limited to a few large, densely settled regions with extensive fixed-rail systems, something relatively rare In che US. In the unlikely event that the USA's existing public transit capacity were tripled and fully utilized, morning private vehicle trips would fall by only 8 percent — certainly a step forward, but hardly enough to end congestion — and tripling public transit capacity would have enormous public spending implications. There are many good reasons to expand the nation's public transit systems to aid mobility, but doing so will not notably reduce either existing or future peak-hour traffic congestion.

Many planners recommend constraints on urban growth. They suggest encouraging population growth within existing neighborhoods which could then be more efficiently served by public transit, although most residents of those neighborhoods vehemently oppose this approach. But in any case, as most regions are already too underpopulated to support much public transit, this strategy would unfortunately have a very limited impact.

The third approach to congestion would be to build sufficient road capacity to accommodate all drivers wanting to travel in peak hours at the same time without delays. But this ‘cure’ is both highly impractical and prohibitively expensive. Governments would have to widen all major commuting roads by, in effect, turning most of every metropolitan region into giant superhighways. Those would then be grossly underutilized during non-peak hours. There are occasions when adding road capacity is sensible, but attempting to build enough to completely eliminate peak-hour congestion is simply futile.

The sole viable option therefore seems to be the acceptance of congestion. Traffic congestion is an absolutely essential mechanism for enabling metropolitan regions throughout the world to cope with excess demands for road space during peak hours each day. Although it can seem intolerable, the alternatives would be even worse. Peak-hour congestion is the balancing mechanism that makes it possible for US citizens to pursue other goals they value, including working or sending their children to school at the same time as their peers, living in low-density settlements, and having a wide choice of places to live and work.

groups.title: Using public transit to reduce US traffic congestion
content: It is sometimes suggested that excess {{31}} on the US road network at certain times of day could be relieved by increasing capacity on public transit. Unfortunately such an approach is unlikely to succeed, as only a minority of commuter {{32}} involve public transit of any type. This is largely because such trips are {{33}} in a small number of places. These are typically urban areas with high population {{34}} already well served by rail.

Even if the costs of both trebling the size of the network and then operating it at full capacity could be met, rush hour traffic would still only decrease by under 10%. While this would represent {{35}}, it would certainly not relieve congestion to any significant degree.
